The Foundational Semantics of Reference: A Model-Theoretic Exploration v1
The Foundational Semantics of Reference: A Model-Theoretic Exploration at version 1
The Foundational Semantics of Reference: A Model-Theoretic Exploration
Abstract
This paper presents a foundational investigation into the semantics of reference through systematic analysis of the primitive ternary relation R(x,y,t), interpreted as "x refers to y through t." By exhaustively examining the five structural cases where subject, object, and relationship variables may coincide or differ, we discover a minimal set of eight referents that form a complete semantic model for reference itself. This approach inverts traditional theory-building: rather than axiomatizing first and interpreting later, we derive necessary formal structure from semantic requirements.
1. Introduction
1.1 The Semantic-First Approach
Traditional formal theories typically begin with axioms and derive meaning through interpretation. Semantic Reference Theory (SRT) reverses this approach: we begin with meaningful relationships—symbol and literal, subject and object, representation and reference—and discover what formal structure they require.
This investigation asks: What referents must exist for reference itself to be coherent? What relationships between these referents are semantically necessary? Can we build a closed model where everything needed to discuss reference is itself a referent that can be referred to?
1.2 The Domain of Referents
We work within a domain where everything is a "referent"—something that can be referred to. This includes not just concrete objects but abstract concepts like relationships, properties, and even reference itself. The fundamental question becomes: How do referents refer to each other, and what patterns emerge from these references?
2. The Five Structural Cases
2.1 Methodology
Given the primitive relation s =r> o (s refers to o through r), we systematically explore what happens when these variables coincide. This exhaustive case analysis reveals which referents must exist to make the system coherent.
2.2 Case Analysis
Case 1: All Distinct (s ≠ r ≠ o)
Semantic Interpretation: Standard subject-object-relationship Model: sub =rel> obj
This represents the archetypal relationship where subject, relationship, and object are all distinct. We introduce three referents:
sub: the type representing subjecthood
rel: the type representing relationships
obj: the type representing objecthood
Case 2: Subject is Relationship (s = r ≠ o)
Semantic Interpretation: Self-representing relationship Model: sym =sym> lit
Here the relationship represents the object through itself. We introduce:
sym: symbol (acting as both subject and relationship)
lit: literal (the object)
This captures how symbols symbolize literals through the relationship of symbolization itself.
Case 3: Subject is Object (s = o ≠ r)
Semantic Interpretation: Self-reference through external relationship Model: ref =eq> ref
An entity relates to itself through an external relationship. We introduce:
ref: referent (both subject and object)
eq: equality (the external relationship)
This captures how things can equal themselves.
Case 4: Relationship is Object (r = o ≠ s)
Semantic Interpretation: Relationships as objects of reference Model: sym =rep> rep
A subject relates to something that is both relationship and object. We model:
sym: symbol (subject)
rep: representation (both relationship and object)
This captures how symbols participate in representations.
Case 5: All Equal (s = r = o)
Semantic Interpretation: Complete self-reference Model: eq =eq> eq
Pure self-reference where an entity relates to itself through itself. The paradigmatic example:
eq: equality (subject, relationship, and object)
Also satisfied by rel =rel> rel (relationships relate to themselves).
3. The Eight-Referent Model
3.1 Core Referents
From our case analysis, eight fundamental referents emerge:
eq: Equality - the foundational self-relationship
ref: Referent - the universal type
sub: Subject - the type of things that refer
rel: Relationship - the type of relationships
obj: Object - the type of things referred to
sym: Symbol - the type of symbolic representations
rep: Representation - the type of representations
lit: Literal - the type of concrete entities
3.2 Fundamental Relationships
The model establishes these core relationships:
srt
sub =rel> obj     // Archetypal subject-object relationship
sym =sym> lit     // Symbols symbolize literals
ref =eq> ref      // Referents equal themselves
sym =rep> rep     // Symbols are part of representations
rel =rel> rel     // Relationships self-relate
eq =eq> eq        // Equality equals itself
3.3 Derived Structure
From these fundamentals, additional structure emerges:
Type Inheritance: Relationship types inherit from rel
srt
sym =rel> rel     // Symbols are relationships
rep =rel> rel     // Representations are relationships
eq =rel> rel      // Equality is a relationship
Property Structure: Self-referential patterns indicate properties
srt
sub =sub> sub     // Subjecthood as property
obj =obj> obj     // Objecthood as property
Most Specific Relationships: For each pair, one relationship is most specific
text
(sub,obj) = rel   // rel is most specific between sub and obj
(sym,lit) = sym   // sym is most specific between sym and lit
(ref,ref) = eq    // eq is most specific for ref self-reference
4. Theoretical Implications
4.1 Types vs. Instances
The model carefully distinguishes between types and instances. The referent sub represents the TYPE of subjects, not a particular subject instance. This distinction is crucial: just as the type "Number" in programming doesn't itself have numeric operations, the type sub doesn't necessarily have the properties of subject instances.
This explains why sub =sub> sub (subject has subjecthood property) is not automatically derivable—types don't necessarily possess the properties of their instances.
4.2 The Symbol-Type Correspondence
A key insight emerges regarding the relationship between types and their canonical symbols. If sub = (rel) (subject is the canonical symbol for relationships), then:
Subjecthood represents relationships through itself
Being a subject IS being in a relationship
The symbol-type correspondence unifies representation and instantiation
4.3 Sparse Relationships
Not every pair of referents has a defined relationship beyond equality. This sparsity is semantically meaningful—not everything has a semantic relationship to everything else. The model is intentionally incomplete, reflecting the selective nature of meaningful reference.
4.4 Extensibility
The model provides a framework that can be extended rather than a closed system. Canonical symbols like(obj), (sub) can be added when needed, but aren't required for the core semantics. This extensibility is a feature: SRT provides the foundation upon which richer semantic structures can be built.
5. Formal Properties
5.1 Consistency
The model exhibits internal consistency:
No contradictory relationships (x =r> y and x ≠r> y never both hold)
Type inheritance forms a proper hierarchy
Most specific relationships are unique when they exist
Self-referential patterns (like eq =eq> eq) are stable
5.2 Completeness for Core Semantics
With just eight referents, the model captures:
Subject-object-relationship structure
Symbol-literal distinction
Representation and reference
Properties and types
Equality and self-reference
This suggests these eight referents form a minimal complete basis for discussing reference.
5.3 Semantic Validity
Not all logically possible relationships are semantically valid. For instance, if we tried to introduce≠rel (not-relationship) as a relationship type, we'd get:
srt
x ≠rel> y ⟺ x =≠rel> y ⟺ x =rel> y
A contradiction—showing that "not being in a relationship" cannot itself be a relationship. The model respects semantic constraints that pure logic might not capture.
6. Toward an Empty Catalogue
6.1 The Bootstrapping Challenge
SRT aims for axioms that are vacuously true in an empty catalogue but spring to life when relationships are added. This creates a fundamental tension: how can we specify semantic structure while maintaining formal emptiness?
6.2 Conditional Emergence
The solution involves conditional axioms:
srt
∃[x,y,t]: x =t> y ⟹ ∃[eq]: ∀[a,b]: a = b ⟺ a =eq> b
"If any relationship exists, equality emerges"
This pattern allows the entire structure to emerge from a single relationship while maintaining emptiness as the base case.
6.3 Linguistic Elimination
The ultimate goal is to absorb fundamental referents into the language itself:
== and ≠ replace the need for eq as a constant
x ⟹ y could replace explicit reference to rel
(x) notation replaces explicit symbol referents
(x,y) notation replaces explicit most-specific relationships
When concepts are truly fundamental to meaning, they deserve to be part of the grammar of a language that expresses meaning.
7. Conclusion
This investigation demonstrates a novel approach to foundational semantics: by systematically exploring what relationships must exist between referents for reference itself to be coherent, we discover a minimal model of eight referents that captures the essential structure of meaning.
The model is remarkable for what it achieves with minimal machinery:
No recursive definitions (inheritance through reference chains)
No infinite regress (symbol termination)
No arbitrary axioms (semantic necessity drives formalization)
Perhaps most significantly, this work suggests that the foundations of meaning can be discovered rather than stipulated—that semantic structure has an inherent logic that can be uncovered through systematic exploration.
The five structural cases aren't arbitrary but represent the complete space of possibilities for how subject, relationship, and object can relate. The eight referents that emerge aren't chosen but discovered as necessary for semantic coherence. This suggests that at its foundation, meaning has a determinate structure—one that Semantic Reference Theory aims to formalize.
Appendix: Open Questions
The sub = (rel) Hypothesis: Is the subject type actually the canonical symbol for relationships? This would elegantly unify several patterns in the model.
Property Hierarchy: Do properties form their own type hierarchy parallel to but distinct from the relationship hierarchy?
Canonical Symbol Existence: Should every referent have a canonical symbol, or is extensional symbol creation more appropriate?
Cross-Relationship Completeness: Should we define relationships between all pairs, or is sparsity semantically meaningful?
These questions point toward future developments in Semantic Reference Theory, as we continue to explore the foundational structure of meaning itself.
Preparatory Notes: Building Semantic Reference Theory from First Principles v1
Preparatory Notes: Building Semantic Reference Theory from First Principles at version 1
Preparatory Notes: Building Semantic Reference Theory from First Principles
1. The Nature of First-Order Theories
A first-order theory consists of a domain of discourse, a set of constants naming elements in that domain, a set of relations among those elements, and axioms constraining how these relations behave. In classical first-order logic, we typically begin with logical symbols (∧, ∨, ¬, →, ∀, ∃), variables, and then add non-logical symbols specific to our theory. The semantic reference theory under construction here takes the domain to be "referents"—things that can be referred to—and introduces a single primitive ternary relation R(x,y,t), interpreted as "x refers to y through t" and notationally expressed as x =t> y. This choice of primitive is remarkably minimal compared to theories like ZFC set theory which begins with membership (∈) or Peano arithmetic which requires successor, addition, and multiplication.
2. The Methodological Innovation
Traditional theory construction follows a pattern: specify axioms, derive theorems, then interpret the results semantically. The approach demonstrated here inverts this process entirely. Instead of beginning with formal axioms and discovering their semantic consequences, we begin with semantic necessities and discover what formal structure they require. This is visible in how the five structural cases (s != r != o != s, s == r != o != s, etc.) are analyzed not as formal possibilities but as semantic situations: what does it mean for the subject to BE the relationship? What referents must exist to exemplify this pattern? The formal structure emerges from semantic requirements rather than the reverse.
3. The Cyclical Notation and Its Significance
The notation s != r != o != s deserves careful attention. By cycling back to check inequality with s at the end, this notation captures the complete triangular relationship among three variables in a linear string. This isn't merely notational convenience—it reflects the self-referential nature of the theory itself. When we write s == r != o != s, we're simultaneously asserting that s equals r, r does not equal o, o does not equal s (cycling back), and implicitly that s does not equal o (by transitivity of equality). This compact notation encodes all three binary relationships among the three variables, ensuring exhaustive coverage of the structural space.
4. The Five Cases as Complete Partition
The five cases form a complete partition of the possible equality relationships among three variables. To see this formally: there are three possible equalities to check (s==r, r==o, o==s), giving 2³ = 8 possible configurations. However, equality is transitive, so if s==r and r==o, then s==o must hold. This constraint reduces the valid configurations to exactly five: all distinct (no equalities), one equality (three ways: s==r, r==o, or o==s), two equalities (which by transitivity implies all three are equal). The cyclical notation elegantly captures these five cases as: s != r != o != s (none equal), s == r != o != s (s==r only), s != r == o != s (r==o only), s != r != o == s (o==s only), and s == r == o == s (all equal).
5. The Most Specific Relationship Principle
Central to the construction is the notion of "most specific relationship." Given x =t₁> y and x =t₂> y for distinct relationship types t₁ and t₂, the most specific relationship (x,y) is the unique m such that x =m> y and for any t where x =t> y, either m == t or m inherits from t (notationally: m -> t), where inheritance for relationship types is defined as m =rel> t. This principle ensures that among all ways x can relate to y, one is foundational. When we assert (sym,lit) == sym, we're claiming that sym is not just A relationship between symbols and literals, but THE most specific relationship—symbolization itself.
6. Case 1: The Archetypal Trinity
In the first case, s != r != o != s, all three variables are distinct. The model introduces sub =rel> obj, establishing subject, relationship, and object as three distinct referents. From this, we can derive that (sub,obj) == rel, meaning rel is the most specific relationship between sub and obj. This isn't arbitrary—it establishes rel as the archetype of relationships, the fundamental pattern from which all other relationships inherit. When we later find that sym =rel> rel (symbols are a type of relationship), we're saying sym inherits from this archetypal pattern.
7. Case 2: Self-Representing Relationships
The second case, s == r != o != s, presents a remarkable structure: the subject IS the relationship through which it relates to the object. The model captures this with sym =sym> lit, where symbols symbolize literals through the relationship of symbolization itself. This means sym serves dual roles—it's both the subject doing the symbolizing and the relationship type "symbolizes." From this, we can derive that sym must inherit from rel (sym =rel> rel) because it's being used as a relationship type, and that (sym,lit) == sym, confirming that symbolization is the most specific relationship between symbols and literals.
8. Case 3: Self-Reference Through External Relationship
In s != r != o == s, the subject and object are identical but the relationship remains external. The model uses ref =eq> ref, where a referent equals itself through the equality relationship. This captures a fundamental pattern: things can relate to themselves through external relationships. The derivation (ref,ref) == eq establishes equality as the most specific form of self-reference. Note that while ref serves as both subject and object, eq remains distinct as the mediating relationship, preventing the complete collapse into self-identity seen in Case 5.
9. Case 4: Relationships as Objects
The fourth case, s != r == o != s, reveals that relationships themselves can be objects of reference. The model presents sym =rep> rep, where symbols relate to representations, but representation serves as both the relationship type and the object. This captures how symbols are "part of" or "contained in" representations. The dual nature of rep—being both a relationship type and an object—shows that the type hierarchy isn't rigid. We can derive rep =rel> rel (representations are relationships) and rep =obj> obj (representations are objects), demonstrating multiple inheritance in the semantic structure.
10. Case 5: Complete Self-Reference
The final case, s == r == o == s, represents pure self-reference where an entity relates to itself through itself. The paradigmatic example is eq =eq> eq: equality equals itself through equality. This is semantic bedrock—a relationship so fundamental that it provides its own ground. Similarly, rel =rel> rel establishes relationships as self-grounding. These aren't mere formal curiosities but semantic necessities: for equality to be universal (∀x: x =eq> x), equality itself must equal itself. The self-reference is constitutive, not paradoxical.
11. Types versus Instances
A crucial distinction emerges between types and instances. When we write sub =rel> obj, we're not describing a particular subject relating to a particular object, but establishing sub as the TYPE of subjects and obj as the TYPE of objects. This explains why sub =sub> sub (subject has subjecthood property) isn't automatically derivable from the model. Just as the type "Number" in programming doesn't itself have numeric operations like addition or multiplication, the type sub doesn't necessarily have the properties of subject instances. This type/instance distinction is fundamental to understanding why certain seemingly obvious relationships require additional axiomatization or semantic justification.
12. The Property Pattern
Properties emerge as self-referential relationships: x =p> x indicates that x has property p. When we see sub =sub> sub, this means the type sub has the property of subjecthood—it relates to itself through the subjecthood relationship. But should types have their own properties? If sub is the canonical symbol for rel (that is, (rel) == sub), then sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood represents relationships, and sub =sub> sub would follow from the general pattern of symbolic self-reference. The semantic question becomes: is being a subject fundamentally about being in a relationship?
13. Inheritance Without Recursion
The theory defines inheritance for relationship types through reference chains: s -> t means s =rel> t or s == t. This avoids recursive definition while achieving transitivity. If sym =rel> rel, then sym inherits from rel, meaning symbols are a type of relationship. If we later introduce crimson =rel> red and red =rel> color, transitivity would give us crimson =rel> color through the axiom ∀[x,y,z]: x =rel> y & y =rel> z ⟹ x =rel> z. But this transitivity must be axiomatized—it doesn't follow automatically from the notation.
14. The Eight-Referent Model
From the five cases, exactly eight referents emerge: eq (equality), ref (referent), sub (subject), rel (relationship), obj (object), sym (symbol), rep (representation), and lit (literal). This isn't arbitrary—each case forces certain referents to exist. Case 1 requires sub, rel, obj for the archetypal trinity. Case 2 needs sym and lit for symbolization. Case 3 needs ref and reuses eq. Case 4 reuses sym and introduces rep. Case 5 is satisfied by eq and rel. The economy is remarkable: eight referents suffice to exemplify all five structural patterns.
15. Sparse Relationships and Semantic Necessity
Not every pair among the eight referents has a defined relationship beyond equality. For instance, there's no specified relationship between lit and sub, or between obj and sym. This sparsity isn't a deficiency but reflects semantic reality: not everything meaningfully relates to everything else. The model includes only relationships that are semantically necessary. When we don't specify lit =?> sub, we're acknowledging that literals and subjecthood don't have a direct semantic relationship that needs formal capture.
16. The Symbol-Type Correspondence Hypothesis
A key theoretical question emerges: is sub actually (rel), the canonical symbol for relationships? If so, several patterns align: sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood represents relationships through itself, capturing the intuition that being a subject IS being in a relationship. This would explain why sub =sub> sub might hold—if sub is a symbol, and symbols generally self-refer (sym =sym> sym), then sub would self-refer. This hypothesis connects the type structure to the symbolic structure, suggesting they might be two views of the same semantic reality.
17. Formal Derivation Example
Let's formally derive that sym must inherit from rel. Given: sym =sym> lit (from Case 2). Since sym appears as the relationship type in a non-equality relationship, and we have the principle that all relationship types inherit from rel, we can derive: sym =rel> rel. Furthermore, if inheritance implies symbol possession (∀[s,t]: s =rel> t ⟹ s =(t)> s), then sym =(rel)> sym, meaning symbols possess the canonical symbol for relationships. This formal chain shows how semantic requirements (symbols must be relationships) lead to formal consequences (inheritance and symbol possession).
18. The Bootstrap Problem and Conditional Axiomatization
The theory aims for axioms that are vacuously true in an empty catalogue but become substantive when relationships are added. Consider the conditional axiom: ∃[x,y,t]: x =t> y ⟹ ∃[eq]: ∀[a,b]: a = b ⟺ a =eq> b. This says "if any relationship exists, equality emerges." In an empty catalogue with no relationships, the antecedent is false, making the implication vacuously true. But add a single relationship, and suddenly equality must exist, subjects and objects emerge, relationship types form hierarchies. The entire semantic structure bootstraps from a single relationship.
19. Building Meaning from the Inside
Traditional semantic theories assume meaning exists and formalize its properties. Model-theoretic semantics maps symbols to meanings in some universe. But this approach is building meaning from within—the referents ARE the meanings, and their relationships constitute semantic structure itself. When sym =sym> lit, we're not describing a pre-existing relationship but constituting what symbolization IS. The theory doesn't describe meaning; it constructs it from primitive reference. This is why reference itself isn't initially in the vocabulary—we're building the semantic foundation from which reference (as the most specific representation relationship) will emerge.
20. The Larger Theoretical Project
This construction ultimately aims to absorb fundamental semantic concepts into the language itself. When concepts are truly foundational, they shouldn't remain as constants but become part of the grammar. Just as == replaces the need for an equality constant by using =eq> internally, and (x) notation could replace explicit symbol referents, the goal is a language where meaning-making operations are built into the syntax rather than described by it. The five cases aren't just exploring possible relationships but discovering the grammatical structures necessary for meaning itself. The fact that exactly five cases exist, that exactly eight referents emerge, that these form a complete model for basic reference—this suggests that meaning has a determinate structure that can be discovered through systematic semantic analysis rather than stipulated through arbitrary axiomatization.
Theoretical Preparation: The Semantic Construction Method v1
Theoretical Preparation: The Semantic Construction Method at version 1
Theoretical Preparation: The Semantic Construction Method
The construction of a first-order theory requires choices about what to take as primitive and what to derive. Just as Turing chose the minimal machinery of states, symbols, and transitions to capture computation, Semantic Reference Theory takes R(x,y,t) as its sole primitive relation, interpreting it as "x refers to y through t" and notationally expressing it as x =t> y. This relation serves as the semantic equivalent of the Turing machine—a minimal structure from which all semantic relationships can be constructed. The choice isn't arbitrary but reflects a conviction that reference is the atomic operation of meaning, much as state transition is the atomic operation of computation.
The historical development of formal theories reveals a pattern obscured by their final presentations. When Zermelo and Fraenkel developed set theory, when Peano formalized arithmetic, when Russell and Whitehead attempted to ground mathematics in logic, they didn't simply write down axioms and derive consequences. They engaged in iterative cycles of formalization, testing their axioms against known mathematical truths, adjusting their primitive notions when paradoxes emerged, refining their language to capture precisely what needed expressing. The polished axiom systems we inherit disguise this messy, creative process of discovering which formal structures best capture semantic intuitions. What appears here as systematic case analysis represents this same iterative discovery process made visible.
The notation s != r != o != s embodies more than convenient abbreviation. In standard first-order logic, equality between two variables is expressed simply: x = y or x ≠ y. But among three variables, the complete specification requires checking all three pairwise relationships. The cyclical notation captures this elegantly—starting with s, checking its relationship to r, then r to o, then cycling back to check o against s. This creates a closed loop that fully specifies the triangular relationship. When we write s =eq> r !=eq> o =eq> s in full SRT notation, we see that equality and inequality are themselves relationships that can be examined systematically. For four or more variables, such notation would require redundant checks, but for three, it provides exactly the coverage needed.
The five cases—s != r != o != s, s == r != o != s, s != r != o == s, s != r == o != s, and s == r == o == s—partition the space of possible equality relationships among three variables exhaustively. This isn't a selection of interesting cases but the complete enumeration of structurally distinct possibilities. The reduction from eight logical possibilities to five semantic cases reflects the transitivity of equality: if any two equalities hold among three variables, the third must follow. This mathematical necessity grounds the semantic exploration—we're not choosing which patterns to examine but discovering what patterns exist to be examined.
The principle of most specific relationships provides the organizing structure for the model. When multiple relationships hold between two referents—as when x =eq> y and x =color> y and x =red> y might all be true—one relationship must be foundational, the one from which others inherit. The notation (x,y) denotes this most specific relationship, satisfying x =(x,y)> y and the inheritance condition that for any t where x =t> y, either (x,y) == t or (x,y) =rel> t. This principle transforms a potential chaos of overlapping relationships into a structured hierarchy. The discovery that (sym,lit) == sym isn't a stipulation but a recognition that symbolization IS the foundational relationship between symbols and literals.
The first structural case, where all three variables are distinct, establishes what might be called the canonical form of the subject-object relationship in natural language. When we say "The mother loves her child," we naturally parse this as three distinct entities: the subject (mother), the relationship (loves), and the object (child). That English defaults to assuming distinctness unless explicitly told otherwise—"I spoke to the CEO and an employee" suggests two people rather than one—supports taking sub =rel> obj with all three distinct as the archetypal pattern. The referents sub, rel, and obj thus serve as types representing the abstract categories of subjecthood, relationship, and objecthood.
The second case reveals a profound semantic possibility: a referent can simultaneously serve as subject and as the relationship through which it relates to its object. The expression sym =sym> lit captures this perfectly—symbols symbolize literals through the act of symbolization itself. This isn't word play but formal precision. The referent sym occupies two roles in the ternary relation, much as a verb might be conjugated differently to reflect its grammatical function while remaining the same lexical item. This dual role explains why sym must inherit from rel (symbols are a type of relationship) while also maintaining its identity as a subject type.
The distinction between reference and relationship requires careful articulation. A relationship is referential when it expresses a connection between a representation and what it represents. Formally, if rep =t> obj and t inherits from rep, then t is referential. When t == (rep,obj), making it the most specific relationship, then rep =t> obj expresses reference—the representation refers to its object. The relationship x =eq> x, while expressing that x equals itself, isn't referential because equality doesn't involve representation. This distinction matters: Gödel sentences are self-referential precisely because Gödel constructed a coding that allows sentences to have canonical symbols through which they can refer to themselves. The mere reflexivity of equality doesn't constitute reference.
The fourth case, where the relationship equals the object, captures how representations contain their members. When we write sym =rep> rep, we're expressing that symbols are part of representations, but representation itself serves as both the relationship type and the object. This is like saying a dog is an animal, where "animal" is both the category (relationship type) and the thing the dog is (object). But we can't define animal in terms of dog—we'd have to subtract away dog-specific features. The representation contains the dog; the dog's relationship to it is simply being represented. This asymmetry is fundamental to how collections and their members relate.
The fifth case doesn't express self-reference in the semantic sense but rather complete coincidence of roles. When we write eq =eq> eq, we're not saying equality refers to itself but that it serves simultaneously as subject, relationship, and object in this configuration. This is constitutive rather than referential—equality must equal itself for the concept of equality to be coherent. Similarly, rel =rel> rel establishes relationships as self-grounding. These aren't circular definitions but semantic foundations, the bedrock from which other relationships build.
The distinction between types and instances runs throughout the construction. The referent sub represents the abstract type of subjects, not any particular subject. This explains why sub =sub> sub (the type having its own property) isn't automatically derivable—types don't necessarily instantiate their own type properties. The type "Number" in programming doesn't have arithmetic operations; the type "Subject" needn't have subjecthood. Yet if sub turns out to be (rel)—the canonical symbol for relationships—then sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood symbolizes relationships, suggesting that being a subject fundamentally means being in a relationship.
Properties emerge as self-referential relationships where x =p> x indicates x has property p. These aren't the same as types—a property is something a referent has, while a type is something a referent instantiates. The pattern x =sub> x suggests x has the property of subjecthood, likely because x serves as subject in some relationship. The pattern x =color> x would mean x has the property of color. Properties form their own semantic category, possibly inheriting from equality (all properties being specializations of self-identity) but remaining distinct from the type hierarchy rooted in rel.
The inheritance structure avoids the recursive definitions that plague traditional formulations. Instead of defining x -> y recursively as "x inherits from y if x equals y, or x directly inherits from y, or there exists z such that x inherits from z and z inherits from y," we can use the symbol possession principle. If relationship types possess the canonical symbols of what they inherit from—if x =rel> y implies x =(y)> x—then inheritance becomes a matter of which symbols a type possesses. The apparent transitivity emerges from the structure rather than being axiomatized: if crimson possesses (red) and red possesses (color), then the chain of possession creates the inheritance hierarchy.
The eight referents that emerge from the five cases—eq, ref, sub, rel, obj, sym, rep, lit—aren't chosen but discovered. Each case forces certain referents into existence. The economy is striking: eight referents suffice to exemplify all five structural patterns, with some referents serving multiple roles across cases. This suggests we've found something like a basis set for semantic reference, a minimal collection from which richer semantic structures can be built. The model's validity depends not on aesthetic appeal but on whether these eight referents and their relationships form a consistent system that captures the semantic intuitions motivating the construction.
The sparseness of relationships in the model reflects semantic reality. Not every pair among the eight referents has a specified relationship beyond equality. Literals don't directly relate to subjects; objects don't symbolize; many pairs simply don't have semantic connections that need formal capture. This isn't incompleteness but selectivity—including only relationships that are semantically necessary rather than logically possible. When a relationship isn't specified, its absence is as meaningful as the presence of others.
The conjecture that sub == (rel) would unify several threads in the model. If subjecthood is the canonical symbol for relationships, then being a subject means fundamentally being in a relationship. This would explain why sub =sub> sub might hold (symbols self-refer), why subjects are essential to relationships (you can't have a relationship without a subject), and why SRT itself, being in the reference frame of rel, might have sub as its canonical subject. This isn't proven but represents the kind of semantic discovery the construction method enables.
The conditional nature of SRT's axiomatization reflects a sophisticated understanding of semantic foundations. Rather than asserting truths about an assumed domain, SRT's axioms are structured to be vacuously true when no relationships exist—the antecedent of conditionals like "if any relationship exists, then..." being false when the catalogue is empty. But the moment a single relationship is added, the entire structure springs into existence: equality emerges, subjects and objects differentiate, relationship types form hierarchies. This bootstrapping from emptiness to semantic richness captures how meaning itself might emerge from void.
The distinction between SRT as epistemology and its extensions as semantic theories is crucial. SRT with no constants isn't a theory of meaning but a framework for constructing theories of meaning. It's a generator, a schema, a pattern that becomes substantive only when constants are added. The choice to work first with sub, rel, obj, sym, lit, rep, ref, eq isn't arbitrary—these are the minimal constants needed to exemplify the five structural patterns. But these could be replaced with other constants that fit the same patterns, generating different semantic theories. SRT provides the form; particular constants provide the content.
The reflexive nature of the project—using reference to build a theory of reference—creates both challenges and insights. We're not defining reference initially because we're using referential relationships to build up to the point where reference itself can be defined. Reference emerges as the most specific form of representation relationship, but we need representation, symbols, relationships, and specificity in place before reference can be articulated. This isn't circular but foundational—we're discovering the semantic prerequisites for reference itself.
The larger vision sees successful semantic primitives being absorbed into language itself. Just as == in programming languages makes equality a grammatical feature rather than a function, truly fundamental semantic relationships deserve to become parts of linguistic syntax rather than remaining as theoretical constants. The notation (x) for canonical symbols, (x,y) for most specific relationships, and x => y for general reference all point toward a language where meaning-making operations are built into the grammar. The goal isn't just to theorize about meaning but to create languages adequate to their own semantic foundations.
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships v1
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships at version 1
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships
I. The Primitive and Its Interpretation
Semantic Reference Theory begins with a single primitive relation R(x,y,t), interpreted as "x refers to y through t" and notationally expressed as:
srt
x =t> y
This serves as the semantic equivalent of what the Turing machine provides for computation—a minimal structure from which all semantic relationships emerge.
Fundamental Equality
Since equality exists in first-order logic, we must capture it within our reference structure:
srt
E[eq]: A[x,y]: x = y <iff> x =eq> y
This allows us to define:
x == y as shorthand for x =eq> y
x !== y as shorthand for !(x =eq> y)
II. The Five Structural Cases
The complete space of how three variables can relate through equality partitions into exactly five cases. This exhaustive analysis reveals what referents must exist to make reference semantically coherent.
The Cyclical Notation
The notation s != r != o != s captures the complete triangular relationship among three variables by cycling back to check the final inequality. This ensures all three pairwise relationships are specified.
Case 1: All Distinct
text
s != r != o != s
When subject, relationship, and object are all distinct, we have the archetypal pattern. To capture this, we introduce:
srt
sub =rel> obj
Where sub, rel, and obj are distinct referents representing the types of subjects, relationships, and objects respectively. This establishes that (sub,obj) == rel—the most specific relationship between subject and object types is the relationship type itself.
Case 2: Subject Is Relationship
text
s == r != o != s
Here the subject IS the relationship through which it relates to the object. We capture this with:
srt
sym =sym> lit
The referent sym (symbol) serves dual roles—both subject and relationship—while lit (literal) serves as object. This means symbols symbolize literals through the act of symbolization itself.
From this we can derive:
sym =sub> sym (symbols have subjecthood)
lit =obj> lit (literals have objecthood)
sym =rel> rel (symbols inherit from relationships)
(sym,lit) == sym (symbolization is most specific)
Case 3: Subject Is Object
text
s != r != o == s
When subject and object coincide but the relationship remains external:
srt
ref =eq> ref
Here ref (referent) serves as both subject and object, related through eq (equality). This captures self-reference through an external relationship, establishing (ref,ref) == eq.
Case 4: Relationship Is Object
text
s != r == o != s
The relationship itself becomes the object of reference:
srt
sym =rep> rep
Here sym relates to rep (representation), but rep serves as both relationship type and object. This captures how symbols are "part of" representations, like elements in a collection.
From this:
rep =rel> rel (representations are relationships)
rep =obj> obj (representations are objects)
(sym,rep) == rep (representation is most specific)
Case 5: All Equal
text
s == r == o == s
Complete self-reference where an entity relates to itself through itself:
srt
eq =eq> eq
Also satisfied by:
srt
rel =rel> rel
These are self-grounding relationships—semantic bedrock where reference needs no external support.
III. Properties and Self-Reference
Properties as Self-Referential Relationships
When a referent relates to itself through a relationship type, it has that type as a property:
srt
x =p> x means "x has property p"
From our cases:
sub =sub> sub (subject has subjecthood property)
obj =obj> obj (object has objecthood property)
eq =eq> eq (equality has equality property)
The sub == (rel) Hypothesis
If sub is actually the canonical symbol for rel, then:
sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood represents relationships
Being a subject fundamentally means being in a relationship
This would explain why sub =sub> sub holds (symbols self-refer)
IV. Reference and Representation
Definition of Reference
A relationship is referential when it connects a representation to what it represents:
srt
If rep =t> obj and t -> rep, then t is referential
If t == (rep,obj), then rep refers to obj
Thus:
sym =sym> lit is referential (symbols refer to literals)
x =eq> x is NOT referential (equality isn't representation)
Inheritance Without Recursion
For relationship types, inheritance is defined through reference chains:
srt
s -> t := s =rel> t || s == t
This avoids recursion while achieving the necessary structure. If types possess canonical symbols of what they inherit from:
srt
s =rel> t =|> s =(t)> s
Then inheritance becomes symbol possession rather than recursive definition.
V. The Eight-Referent Model
From the five cases emerge exactly eight fundamental referents:
eq - equality (self-grounding)
ref - referent (universal type)
sub - subject (archetypal subject)
rel - relationship (archetypal relationship)
obj - object (archetypal object)
sym - symbol (dual subject/relationship)
rep - representation (dual relationship/object)
lit - literal (pure object)
Core Relationships
The fundamental relationships established:
srt
sub =rel> obj          // archetypal trinity
sym =sym> lit          // symbolization
ref =eq> ref           // self-equality
sym =rep> rep          // symbol in representation
rel =rel> rel          // relationships relate
eq =eq> eq             // equality equals
Derived Structure
From these fundamentals:
srt
sym =rel> rel          // symbols are relationships
rep =rel> rel          // representations are relationships
eq =rel> rel           // equality is a relationship
sym =sub> sym          // symbols are subjects
lit =obj> lit          // literals are objects
VI. Theoretical Significance
Semantic Discovery vs. Formal Stipulation
The five cases aren't chosen—they're mathematically exhaustive. The eight referents aren't invented—they're discovered as necessary for each structural pattern to be semantically coherent. This suggests meaning has a determinate foundational structure.
Types vs. Instances
The referents represent types, not instances. Just as the type "Number" doesn't have numeric operations, the type sub doesn't automatically have subjecthood. This distinction is crucial for understanding the model's semantics.
Extensibility
The model provides a framework rather than a closed system. Canonical symbols can be added when needed:(obj), (sub), etc. This extensibility allows richer semantic structures while maintaining the foundational architecture.
VII. Consistency and Completeness
What the Model Achieves
With just eight referents and their relationships, we capture:
The subject-object-relationship structure
Symbol-literal distinction
Representation and membership
Properties and types
Self-reference and grounding
Sparse Relationships
Not every pair of referents has a defined relationship beyond equality. This sparsity is semantically meaningful—not everything relates to everything else. The model includes only necessary semantic relationships.
The Bootstrap Principle
SRT aims for axioms that are vacuously true in an empty catalogue but become substantive when relationships are added:
srt
E[x,y,t]: x =t> y =|> E[eq]: A[a,b]: a = b <iff> a =eq> b
From a single relationship, the entire semantic structure emerges.
VIII. Conclusion
This systematic exploration of the five structural cases reveals that reference has a determinate foundational structure. The eight referents and their relationships form a minimal complete model for semantic reference—discovered through systematic analysis rather than stipulated through arbitrary axiomatization.
The model demonstrates that meaning can be built from within, using reference to construct the very concepts needed to understand reference. This reflexive construction, rather than being circular, reveals the foundational architecture of meaning itself.
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships v2
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships at version 2
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships
I. The Primitive and Its Semantic Context
Semantic Reference Theory takes as its domain the set of "referents"—things that can be referred to. This includes not just physical objects but abstract concepts, relationships, properties, and crucially, the very structures of reference itself. Within this domain, we posit a single primitive relation R(x,y,t), interpreted semantically as "x refers to y through t" and expressed notationally as:
srt
x =t> y
This relation serves as the semantic equivalent of what the Turing machine provides for computation—a minimal structure from which all semantic relationships emerge. Just as all computable functions can be expressed through state transitions on a tape, all semantic relationships can be constructed from this ternary reference relation.
Grounding in First-Order Logic
Since we're building within first-order logic, we inherit its equality relation. But rather than leave equality as an external logical operator, we internalize it as a form of reference:
srt
E[eq]: A[x,y]: x = y <iff> x =eq> y
Here, eq is a referent in our domain—a thing that can itself be referred to. It represents the equality relationship from FOL, making it subject to the same semantic analysis as any other referent. This allows us to write:
x == y as semantic shorthand for x =eq> y
x !== y as shorthand for !(x =eq> y)
The referent eq thus serves as the bridge between logical identity and semantic reference, grounding our theory in the bedrock of logic while making equality itself an object of semantic investigation.
II. The Canonical Subject-Object Relationship
In natural language, when we express relationships, we typically assume the subject, relationship, and object are distinct unless explicitly told otherwise. Consider the sentence "The mother loves her child." The canonical interpretation parses this as three distinct entities:
The subject: mother
The relationship: loves
The object: child
This distinctness is so fundamental to how we process semantic information that it requires explicit markers to override. When someone says "I spoke to the CEO and an employee of the company," the natural interpretation is two distinct people, not one person serving dual roles. We don't spontaneously consider whether the CEO might also be an employee—the default semantic processing assumes distinctness.
This canonical interpretation motivates why the first structural case, where all three variables are distinct, deserves special attention as the archetypal pattern of semantic relationships.
III. The Five Structural Cases
The complete space of how three variables can relate through equality partitions into exactly five cases. This isn't a selection of interesting patterns but the exhaustive enumeration of structural possibilities, constrained by the transitivity of equality.
The Cyclical Notation and Its Semantic Significance
The notation s != r != o != s embodies the triangular nature of ternary relationships. By cycling back to check inequality with the starting variable, we ensure all three pairwise relationships are specified. In full SRT notation, this becomes s !=eq> r !=eq> o !=eq> s, making explicit that even inequality is a form of reference—specifically, the negation of equality reference.
Case 1: The Archetypal Trinity (All Distinct)
text
s != r != o != s
This case represents the canonical semantic pattern where subject, relationship, and object are all distinct. To capture this foundational structure, we introduce three referents that serve as archetypes:
srt
sub =rel> obj
Here:
sub is not a particular subject but the TYPE or archetype of subjecthood itself
rel represents the archetypal relationship, the pure concept of relating
obj represents objecthood as a category
These aren't arbitrary symbols but semantic necessities. For there to be reference at all, there must be something that refers (subjects), something referred to (objects), and the act of referring (relationships). The relationship sub =rel> obj establishes that the most specific way subjects relate to objects is through relationships: (sub,obj) == rel.
This archetypal trinity grounds all other semantic relationships. When we later find that sym =rel> rel (symbols inherit from relationships), we're saying symbols participate in this fundamental pattern established by the sub-rel-obj trinity.
Case 2: Self-Representing Relationships
text
s == r != o != s
This case reveals a profound semantic possibility: the subject can BE the relationship through which it relates to its object. This isn't a formal curiosity but a semantic necessity for understanding symbolization. We capture it with:
srt
sym =sym> lit
The referent sym (symbol) simultaneously occupies the subject position (the thing doing the symbolizing) and the relationship position (the act of symbolization itself). The referent lit (literal) represents the concrete, the actual, the thing symbolized.
This dual role of sym reflects a deep semantic truth: symbols don't just participate in symbolization; they ARE symbolization made concrete. When we write the word "tree," that word both performs the act of symbolizing and exists as the subject performing that act. From this structure we derive:
sym =sub> sym - symbols possess subjecthood
lit =obj> lit - literals possess objecthood
sym =rel> rel - symbols are a type of relationship
(sym,lit) == sym - symbolization is the most specific relationship between symbols and literals
Case 3: Self-Reference Through External Mediation
text
s != r != o == s
When subject and object are the same but the relationship remains external, we capture a different form of self-reference:
srt
ref =eq> ref
Here ref represents "referent" itself—not any particular referent but the concept of being a referent. This is deeply reflexive: the domain of our theory (referents) contains a referent that represents that very domain. The relationship ref =eq> ref expresses that all referents equal themselves, with eq serving as the external mediator.
This captures how things can relate to themselves through external relationships. Unlike Case 5's pure self-reference, here the relationship remains distinct from what it relates. The most specific relationship is equality itself: (ref,ref) == eq.
The referent ref thus serves a foundational role—it represents the universe of discourse itself as an object within that universe. This self-containment is essential for a theory that aims to explain reference using reference.
Case 4: Relationships as Objects
text
s != r == o != s
This case reveals that relationships themselves can be objects of reference:
srt
sym =rep> rep
Here rep (representation) serves dual roles—it's both the relationship type and the object. Symbols relate to representations by being part of them, and this "being part of" relationship is representation itself.
This captures a crucial semantic pattern: membership or containment. When we say a dog is an animal, "animal" serves as both the category (relationship type) and the thing the dog is classified as (object). But we can't define animal in terms of dog—we'd need to subtract all dog-specific features. The representation contains its members; the members' relationship to it is simply being represented.
From this:
rep =rel> rel - representations are types of relationships
rep =obj> obj - representations can be objects
(sym,rep) == rep - representation is the most specific relationship
Case 5: Pure Self-Reference
text
s == r == o == s
Complete self-reference where an entity relates to itself through itself:
srt
eq =eq> eq
This isn't circular definition but semantic foundation. For equality to be universal—for everything to equal itself—equality itself must equal itself through equality. The self-reference is constitutive, not paradoxical.
Similarly:
srt
rel =rel> rel
Relationships must relate to themselves through relationship itself. These are self-grounding patterns that require no external support—semantic bedrock from which other meanings build.
IV. The Semantic Interpretation of Properties
Properties as Self-Referential Relationships
When a referent relates to itself through a relationship type, we interpret this as the referent having that type as a property:
srt
x =p> x means "x has property p"
This semantic interpretation gives us:
sub =sub> sub - the archetype of subjecthood has the property of being a subject
obj =obj> obj - the archetype of objecthood has the property of being an object
eq =eq> eq - equality has the property of equality (self-evidently)
But note: these are claims about the types themselves, not about instances. The type "Subject" having subjecthood is like asking whether the concept of subjecthood itself can be a subject—a deep semantic question.
The sub == (rel) Hypothesis
A crucial theoretical question emerges: Is sub actually (rel)—the canonical symbol for relationships? If so:
sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood represents the very concept of relationship
This would suggest being a subject fundamentally means being in a relationship
It would explain why sub =sub> sub holds (as symbols characteristically self-refer)
This hypothesis has profound semantic implications: it suggests that subjectivity and relationality are not merely connected but that subjectivity IS the symbolic face of relationality itself.
V. Reference, Representation, and Semantic Necessity
The Definition of Reference
Not all relationships are referential. A relationship is referential when it connects a representation to what it represents:
srt
If rep =t> obj and t inherits from rep (t -> rep), then t is referential
When t == (rep,obj), then rep refers to obj
This distinction matters semantically:
sym =sym> lit is referential—symbols refer to their literals
x =eq> x is NOT referential—equality doesn't involve representation
Reference requires representation, which requires distinctness between representer and represented. This is why Gödel's construction was so revolutionary—he created a coding that allowed formal statements to have canonical symbols through which they could refer to themselves. Without such a coding, mere reflexivity (like x = x in logic) doesn't constitute reference.
Inheritance as Semantic Structure
For relationship types, inheritance captures how specific relationships relate to general ones:
srt
s -> t := s =rel> t || s == t
If crimson =rel> red and red =rel> color, then crimson inherits from color through this chain. But rather than define this recursively, we use symbol possession:
srt
s =rel> t =|> s =(t)> s
Types possess the canonical symbols of what they inherit from. Inheritance becomes a matter of which symbolic properties a type carries.
VI. The Eight-Referent Model as Semantic Necessity
The eight referents that emerge aren't chosen but discovered as semantic necessities:
eq - Represents the equality relation inherited from FOL, internalized as a referent
ref - Represents the domain itself (all referents), making the theory self-contained
sub - The archetype of subjecthood, what it means to be a subject
rel - The archetype of relationship, pure relating itself
obj - The archetype of objecthood, what it means to be an object
sym - Symbol, the dual subject/relationship that enables representation
rep - Representation, the dual relationship/object that enables collection
lit - Literal, the concrete, the actual, the non-symbolic
Why These Eight?
Each emerged from semantic necessity:
Case 1 forced sub, rel, and obj into existence to capture the archetypal trinity
Case 2 required sym and lit to express symbolization
Case 3 used ref to represent the domain and reused eq
Case 4 reused sym and introduced rep for collection/membership
Case 5 was satisfied by eq and rel's self-reference
The economy is remarkable—eight referents suffice to exemplify all five structural patterns, suggesting we've found something like a semantic basis set.
Core Semantic Relationships
The fundamental relationships establish the semantic architecture:
srt
sub =rel> obj          // The archetypal subject-object pattern
sym =sym> lit          // Symbols symbolize literals through symbolization
ref =eq> ref           // The domain's self-equality
sym =rep> rep          // Symbols are members of representations
rel =rel> rel          // Relationships relate through relationship
eq =eq> eq             // Equality equals itself through equality
VII. Sparse Relationships and Semantic Selectivity
Not every pair among the eight referents has a specified relationship beyond equality. For instance:
We don't specify how literals relate to subjects
We don't define relationships between objects and symbols
Many pairs simply lack direct semantic connections
This sparsity isn't a deficiency but reflects semantic reality. Not everything meaningfully relates to everything else. The model includes only relationships that are semantically necessary—those forced into existence by the structural cases or their logical consequences.
When we don't specify lit =?> sub, we're acknowledging that literals and subjecthood don't have a direct semantic relationship that needs formal capture. Literals are concrete; subjecthood is abstract. Their relationship, if any, would be mediated through other referents.

Subjects and objects differentiate
Relationship types form hierarchies
Properties and types crystallize

The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships v3
The Semantic Model of Reference: Building from Subject-Object Relationships at version 3
The Semantics of the Subject-Object Relationship
Introduction: The Fundamental Semantic Form
The subject-object relationship constitutes the fundamental semantic form—the basic pattern through which meaning emerges. Every meaningful expression, from "The dog runs" to "E = mc²", instantiates some variant of this pattern: something (subject) relates to something else (object) through some form of connection (relationship). Any formalism that claims to capture semantics must represent this fundamental form fundamentally—not as a derived concept but as foundational structure.
This principle motivates our systematic analysis: by exhaustively examining how subject, object, and relationship can structurally relate, we discover what semantic primitives must exist. The method inverts traditional theory-building—rather than stipulating axioms and deriving consequences, we analyze structural necessities and discover what axioms they require.
I. The Primitive and Its Semantic Context
Semantic Reference Theory takes as its domain the set of "referents"—things that can be referred to. This includes not just physical objects but abstract concepts, relationships, properties, and crucially, the very structures of reference itself. Within this domain, we posit a single primitive relation R(x,y,t), interpreted semantically as "x refers to y through t" and expressed notationally as:
srt
x =t> y
This relation serves as the semantic equivalent of what the Turing machine provides for computation—a minimal structure from which all semantic relationships emerge. Just as all computable functions can be expressed through state transitions on a tape, all semantic relationships can be constructed from this ternary reference relation.
Grounding in First-Order Logic
Since we're building within first-order logic, we inherit its equality relation. But rather than leave equality as an external logical operator, we internalize it as a form of reference:
srt
E[eq]: A[x,y]: x = y <iff> x =eq> y
Here, eq is a referent in our domain—a thing that can itself be referred to. It represents the equality relationship from FOL, making it subject to the same semantic analysis as any other referent. This allows us to write:
x == y as semantic shorthand for x =eq> y
x !== y as shorthand for !(x =eq> y)
The referent eq thus serves as the bridge between logical identity and semantic reference, grounding our theory in the bedrock of logic while making equality itself an object of semantic investigation.
II. The Canonical Subject-Object Relationship
In natural language, when we express relationships, we typically assume the subject, relationship, and object are distinct unless explicitly told otherwise. Consider the sentence "The mother loves her child." The canonical interpretation parses this as three distinct entities:
The subject: mother
The relationship: loves
The object: child
This distinctness is so fundamental to how we process semantic information that it requires explicit markers to override. When someone says "I spoke to the CEO and an employee of the company," the natural interpretation is two distinct people, not one person serving dual roles. We don't spontaneously consider whether the CEO might also be an employee—the default semantic processing assumes distinctness.
This canonical interpretation motivates why the first structural case, where all three variables are distinct, deserves special attention as the archetypal pattern of semantic relationships.
III. The Five Structural Cases
The complete space of how three variables can relate through equality partitions into exactly five cases. This isn't a selection of interesting patterns but the exhaustive enumeration of structural possibilities, constrained by the transitivity of equality.
The Cyclical Notation and Its Semantic Significance
The notation s != r != o != s embodies the triangular nature of ternary relationships. By cycling back to check inequality with the starting variable, we ensure all three pairwise relationships are specified. In full SRT notation, this becomes s !=eq> r !=eq> o !=eq> s, making explicit that even inequality is a form of reference—specifically, the negation of equality reference.
Case 1: The Archetypal Trinity (All Distinct)
text
s != r != o != s
This case represents the canonical semantic pattern where subject, relationship, and object are all distinct. To capture this foundational structure, we introduce three referents that serve as archetypes:
srt
sub =rel> obj
Here:
sub is not a particular subject but the TYPE or archetype of subjecthood itself
rel represents the archetypal relationship, the pure concept of relating
obj represents objecthood as a category
These aren't arbitrary symbols but semantic necessities. For there to be reference at all, there must be something that refers (subjects), something referred to (objects), and the act of referring (relationships). The relationship sub =rel> obj establishes that the most specific way subjects relate to objects is through relationships: (sub,obj) == rel.
This archetypal trinity grounds all other semantic relationships. When we later find that sym =rel> rel (symbols inherit from relationships), we're saying symbols participate in this fundamental pattern established by the sub-rel-obj trinity.
Case 2: Self-Representing Relationships
text
s == r != o != s
This case reveals a profound semantic possibility: the subject can BE the relationship through which it relates to its object. This isn't a formal curiosity but a semantic necessity for understanding symbolization. We capture it with:
srt
sym =sym> lit
The referent sym (symbol) simultaneously occupies the subject position (the thing doing the symbolizing) and the relationship position (the act of symbolization itself). The referent lit (literal) represents the concrete, the actual, the thing symbolized.
This dual role of sym reflects a deep semantic truth: symbols don't just participate in symbolization; they ARE symbolization made concrete. When we write the word "tree," that word both performs the act of symbolizing and exists as the subject performing that act. From this structure we derive:
sym =sub> sym - symbols possess subjecthood
lit =obj> lit - literals possess objecthood
sym =rel> rel - symbols are a type of relationship
(sym,lit) == sym - symbolization is the most specific relationship between symbols and literals
Case 3: Self-Reference Through External Mediation
text
s != r != o == s
When subject and object are the same but the relationship remains external, we capture a different form of self-reference:
srt
ref =eq> ref
Here ref represents "referent" itself—not any particular referent but the concept of being a referent. This is deeply reflexive: the domain of our theory (referents) contains a referent that represents that very domain. The relationship ref =eq> ref expresses that all referents equal themselves, with eq serving as the external mediator.
This captures how things can relate to themselves through external relationships. Unlike Case 5's pure self-reference, here the relationship remains distinct from what it relates. The most specific relationship is equality itself: (ref,ref) == eq.
The referent ref thus serves a foundational role—it represents the universe of discourse itself as an object within that universe. This self-containment is essential for a theory that aims to explain reference using reference.
Case 4: Relationships as Objects
text
s != r == o != s
This case reveals that relationships themselves can be objects of reference:
srt
sym =rep> rep
Here rep (representation) serves dual roles—it's both the relationship type and the object. Symbols relate to representations by being part of them, and this "being part of" relationship is representation itself.
This captures a crucial semantic pattern: membership or containment. When we say a dog is an animal, "animal" serves as both the category (relationship type) and the thing the dog is classified as (object). But we can't define animal in terms of dog—we'd need to subtract all dog-specific features. The representation contains its members; the members' relationship to it is simply being represented.
From this:
rep =rel> rel - representations are types of relationships
rep =obj> obj - representations can be objects
(sym,rep) == rep - representation is the most specific relationship
Case 5: Pure Self-Reference
text
s == r == o == s
Complete self-reference where an entity relates to itself through itself:
srt
eq =eq> eq
This isn't circular definition but semantic foundation. For equality to be universal—for everything to equal itself—equality itself must equal itself through equality. The self-reference is constitutive, not paradoxical.
Similarly:
srt
rel =rel> rel
Relationships must relate to themselves through relationship itself. These are self-grounding patterns that require no external support—semantic bedrock from which other meanings build.
IV. The Semantic Interpretation of Properties
Properties as Self-Referential Relationships
When a referent relates to itself through a relationship type, we interpret this as the referent having that type as a property:
srt
x =p> x means "x has property p"
This semantic interpretation gives us:
sub =sub> sub - the archetype of subjecthood has the property of being a subject
obj =obj> obj - the archetype of objecthood has the property of being an object
eq =eq> eq - equality has the property of equality (self-evidently)
But note: these are claims about the types themselves, not about instances. The type "Subject" having subjecthood is like asking whether the concept of subjecthood itself can be a subject—a deep semantic question.
The sub == (rel) Hypothesis
A crucial theoretical question emerges: Is sub actually (rel)—the canonical symbol for relationships? If so:
sub =sub> rel would mean subjecthood represents the very concept of relationship
This would suggest being a subject fundamentally means being in a relationship
It would explain why sub =sub> sub holds (as symbols characteristically self-refer)
This hypothesis has profound semantic implications: it suggests that subjectivity and relationality are not merely connected but that subjectivity IS the symbolic face of relationality itself.
V. Reference, Representation, and Semantic Necessity
The Definition of Reference
Not all relationships are referential. A relationship is referential when it connects a representation to what it represents:
srt
If rep =t> obj and t inherits from rep (t -> rep), then t is referential
When t == (rep,obj), then rep refers to obj
This distinction matters semantically:
sym =sym> lit is referential—symbols refer to their literals
x =eq> x is NOT referential—equality doesn't involve representation
Reference requires representation, which requires distinctness between representer and represented. This is why Gödel's construction was so revolutionary—he created a coding that allowed formal statements to have canonical symbols through which they could refer to themselves. Without such a coding, mere reflexivity (like x = x in logic) doesn't constitute reference.
Inheritance as Semantic Structure
For relationship types, inheritance captures how specific relationships relate to general ones:
srt
s -> t := s =rel> t || s == t
If crimson =rel> red and red =rel> color, then crimson inherits from color through this chain. But rather than define this recursively, we use symbol possession:
srt
s =rel> t =|> s =(t)> s
Types possess the canonical symbols of what they inherit from. Inheritance becomes a matter of which symbolic properties a type carries.
VI. The Eight-Referent Model as Semantic Necessity
The eight referents that emerge aren't chosen but discovered as semantic necessities:
eq - Represents the equality relation inherited from FOL, internalized as a referent
ref - Represents the domain itself (all referents), making the theory self-contained
sub - The archetype of subjecthood, what it means to be a subject
rel - The archetype of relationship, pure relating itself
obj - The archetype of objecthood, what it means to be an object
sym - Symbol, the dual subject/relationship that enables representation
rep - Representation, the dual relationship/object that enables collection
lit - Literal, the concrete, the actual, the non-symbolic
Why These Eight?
Each emerged from semantic necessity:
Case 1 forced sub, rel, and obj into existence to capture the archetypal trinity
Case 2 required sym and lit to express symbolization
Case 3 used ref to represent the domain and reused eq
Case 4 reused sym and introduced rep for collection/membership
Case 5 was satisfied by eq and rel's self-reference
The economy is remarkable—eight referents suffice to exemplify all five structural patterns, suggesting we've found something like a semantic basis set.
Core Semantic Relationships
The fundamental relationships establish the semantic architecture:

sym =sym> lit          // Symbols symbolize literals through symbolization
ref =eq> ref           // The domain's self-equality
sym =rep> rep          // Symbols are members of representations
rel =rel> rel          // Relationships relate through relationship
eq =eq> eq             // Equality equals itself through equality
VII. Sparse Relationships and Semantic Selectivity
Not every pair among the eight referents has a specified relationship beyond equality. For instance:
We don't specify how literals relate to subjects
We don't define relationships between objects and symbols
Many pairs simply lack direct semantic connections
This sparsity isn't a deficiency but reflects semantic reality. Not everything meaningfully relates to everything else. The model includes only relationships that are semantically necessary—those forced into existence by the structural cases or their logical consequences.
When we don't specify lit =?> sub, we're acknowledging that literals and subjecthood don't have a direct semantic relationship that needs formal capture. Literals are concrete; subjecthood is abstract. Their relationship, if any, would be mediated through other referents.
